content: Potassium citrate is a urinary alkalinizer approved by the FDA for the treatment of nephrolithiasis. Common side effects include abdominal discomfort, vomiting, diarrhea, loose bowel movements, or nausea. Adult Indications and Dosage FDA-Labeled Indications: Renal tubular acidosis (RTA) with calcium stones. Hypocitraturic calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis of any etiology. Uric acid lithiasis with or without calcium stones. Dosage: Therapy should begin at 60 mEq per day, divided into doses of 30 mEq twice daily or 20 mEq three times daily, taken with meals or within 30 minutes after meals or a bedtime snack. Alternatively, therapy can start at 30 mEq per day, divided into doses of 15 mEq twice daily or 10 mEq three times daily, taken with meals or within 30 minutes after meals or a bedtime snack. Off-Label Use: Limited information is available regarding off-label guideline-supported or non-guideline-supported use of potassium citrate in adults. Pediatric Indications and Dosage FDA-Labeled Indications: Safety and efficacy in pediatric patients have not been established. Off-Label Use: Limited information is available regarding off-label use in pediatric patients. Contraindications Potassium citrate is contraindicated in the following situations: Patients with hyperkalemia or conditions predisposing to hyperkalemia (e.g., chronic renal failure, uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, acute dehydration, adrenal insufficiency, or use of potassium-sparing agents like spironolactone). Patients with delayed gastric emptying, esophageal compression, intestinal obstruction, or strictures, as these conditions may delay tablet passage through the gastrointestinal tract. Patients with peptic ulcer disease due to its ulcerogenic potential. Patients with active urinary tract infections caused by urea-splitting or other organisms, as bacterial enzymatic degradation of citrate may reduce its effectiveness and increase urinary pH, promoting bacterial growth. Warnings Hyperkalemia: Potassium citrate can cause hyperkalemia and cardiac arrest in patients with impaired potassium excretion mechanisms. Hyperkalemia may develop rapidly and be asymptomatic, with manifestations such as peaked T-waves, loss of P-waves, and prolonged QT intervals on ECG. Avoid use in patients with chronic renal failure or conditions impairing potassium excretion. Monitor serum potassium levels and ECGs periodically. Gastrointestinal Lesions: Solid dosage forms of potassium salts, including potassium citrate, may cause gastrointestinal irritation, ulceration, or stenosis. Discontinue use immediately if severe vomiting, abdominal pain, or gastrointestinal bleeding occurs, and investigate for bowel perforation or obstruction. Adverse Reactions Clinical Trials: Limited information is available regarding adverse reactions in clinical trials. Postmarketing Experience: Minor gastrointestinal complaints such as abdominal discomfort, vomiting, diarrhea, loose stools, or nausea may occur. These symptoms can often be alleviated by taking the medication with meals or snacks or by reducing the dosage. Drug Interactions Potassium-Sparing Diuretics: Avoid concomitant use with potassium-sparing diuretics (e.g., spironolactone, triamterene) as this may lead to severe hyperkalemia. Drugs Slowing Gastrointestinal Transit Time: Agents like anticholinergics may increase gastrointestinal irritation caused by potassium salts. Use in Specific Populations Pregnancy: Pregnancy Category C (FDA): Animal reproduction studies have not been conducted. Use only if clearly needed. No Australian guidance is available. Nursing Mothers: The effect of potassium citrate on potassium ion content in human milk is unknown. Use only if clearly needed. Pediatric Use: Safety and efficacy in children have not been established. Geriatric Use: No specific FDA guidance is available for geriatric populations. Renal Impairment: Potassium citrate may be less effective in patients with severe renal tubular acidosis or chronic diarrheal syndrome due to low urinary citrate levels. Higher doses may be required. Hepatic Impairment: No specific FDA guidance is available for patients with hepatic impairment. Administration and Monitoring Administration: Take tablets whole without crushing, chewing, or sucking. Follow the prescribed dosage, especially if taking diuretics or digitalis preparations. Monitoring: Regularly monitor serum electrolytes, serum creatinine, and complete blood counts every four months. Perform periodic ECGs. Discontinue treatment if hyperkalemia, significant serum creatinine elevation, or a significant drop in hemoglobin/hematocrit occurs. Overdosage Hyperkalemia is the primary concern in overdose situations. Symptoms may include muscle paralysis and cardiovascular collapse. Treatment includes monitoring for arrhythmias, discontinuing potassium-containing medications, and administering therapies such as intravenous calcium gluconate, insulin with dextrose, sodium bicarbonate, or dialysis. Pharmacology Mechanism of Action: Potassium citrate increases urinary pH and citrate levels, reducing the crystallization of stone-forming salts like calcium oxalate, calcium phosphate, and uric acid. Pharmacokinetics: Oral administration leads to an alkaline load, increasing urinary pH and citrate excretion. Effects on urinary citrate begin within the first hour and last up to 12 hours. Clinical Studies Potassium citrate has been shown to reduce stone formation rates in patients with renal tubular acidosis and hypocitraturic calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis. Long-term studies indicate its effectiveness in preventing new stone formation and maintaining high urinary citrate levels. Patient Counseling Information Advise patients to take tablets as directed, without crushing or chewing. Inform patients to report any difficulty swallowing, tarry stools, or signs of gastrointestinal bleeding. Emphasize the importance of regular blood tests and ECGs to ensure safety. Storage Store in a tightly sealed container. Brand Names Urocit-K 10, Urocit-K 5, Urocit-K 15.
